summary: Defines extensions to FTP that add optional security, such as authentication and protection of the data and commands sent over a connection. These are new commands and replies that clients and servers can negotiate.

plainLanguage.summary: Regular file transfer is like a postcard anyone can read. This adds a way to prove who you are and seal the message.

questions: what are the ftp security extensions
what is the ftp auth command
what does ftp prot command do
subtitle: Optional FTP commands that add authentication, integrity and encryption to the control and data channels.

tldr.problem: Plain FTP sends usernames and passwords in cleartext, and nothing protects commands, replies or file data from being read, altered or injected by someone on the network.
tldr.mechanism: New optional commands (AUTH, ADAT, PBSZ, PROT, CCC, MIC, CONF, ENC) let client and server run a security exchange, then wrap commands, replies and data blocks in integrity and confidentiality protection.
tldr.outcome: None of the commands is required, and the RFC leaves policy to implementations. Third-party transfers between two servers cannot be secured with these extensions.

facts.label: New commands
facts.value: AUTH, ADAT, PBSZ, PROT, CCC, MIC, CONF, ENC

today: RFC 2228 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 959. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why FTP Needed Security Extensions
sections.content:
FTP as defined in RFC 959 authenticates users with the USER and PASS commands, and the password travels in cleartext. Anyone monitoring a local or wide-area network can steal it. FTP also has no way to encrypt or verify the authenticity of commands, replies or transferred data, so an active attacker could modify data, start spurious transfers or invoke other commands on the server.

The RFC lists the practices of the time for sending files securely: pre-encrypted files with manually distributed keys, email, a PEM message, or rcp enhanced with Kerberos. None was a standard, and none was truly interactive. It also explains why Telnet's authentication and encryption option does not help: RFC 1123 forbids Telnet option negotiation on the FTP control connection, and that option cannot give integrity without confidentiality or protect the data channel.

RFC 2228 updates RFC 959 with strong authentication, integrity and confidentiality on both the control and data channels. It is compatible with RFC 959, and none of the new commands is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Old file transfer is like shouting your password across a crowded room. This RFC adds a private whisper and a seal so nobody can read or tamper with what you send.

sections.title: How the Security Interaction Works
sections.content:
The extensions give FTP an abstract mechanism for authenticating connections and for protecting commands, replies and data. Authentication establishes the identity of the client and/or server. Authorization is validating a user for login, which in plain FTP rests on USER, PASS and ACCT.

The interaction starts when the client names a security mechanism with AUTH. The server accepts it, rejects it, or (if it does not know the extensions at all) rejects the command completely. The client can try several mechanisms until one is accepted, which is a rudimentary form of negotiation. If the mechanism needs more data, the two sides exchange blocks of security data with ADAT until the exchange completes. The result is a security association, which may include authentication (client, server or mutual) and keys for integrity and confidentiality.

The wording is deliberate: a security association might include no authentication at all. A Diffie-Hellman exchange sets up a secret key without authenticating anyone, and a server with an RSA key pair can authenticate itself to a client that has none.

The RFC does not set policy. A server might insist on a security mechanism instead of a password, require integrity on the command channel, or require some files to be sent encrypted. An anonymous client might refuse downloads without integrity protection.
sections.plainLanguage: First the two programs agree on a secret handshake. Once they both know it, they can use it to prove who they are and to seal their messages.

sections.title: AUTH, ADAT and Login
sections.content:
AUTH carries a case-insensitive mechanism name. Names must be registered with the IANA, except that names beginning with X- are reserved for local use. The server answers with a reply code that says what happened:

  • 234: mechanism accepted, no security data needed.
  • 334: mechanism accepted, security data required (the reply may carry some).
  • 504: mechanism not understood. 534: not willing, for policy reasons. 431: not able, for example a required resource is unavailable.
  • 500: the server does not recognize AUTH. 502: it recognizes it but does not implement the extensions.

A second AUTH, if accepted, removes any state from earlier security commands and forces the user to authorize again.

ADAT carries base 64 encoded security data specific to the mechanism. It must follow a successful AUTH and cannot be reissued after an exchange completes unless AUTH resets the state. A 335 reply means more data is needed, and 235 means the exchange succeeded. A server that rejects the data (a failed checksum, for instance) answers 535. Servers may return data to the client as ADAT=base64data in the reply text. The RFC strongly recommends that mechanisms provide sequencing on the command channel so commands cannot be deleted, reordered or replayed.

Login changes slightly. A username from USER is always required. If the server is willing to log the user in based on the identity from the security exchange, it replies 232. If the mechanism uses a challenge/response password, it replies 336 with the challenge in the text, and the client must show the challenge to the user before asking for the password.
sections.plainLanguage: AUTH is asking, can we use this secret code? ADAT is the back-and-forth where the two sides swap the pieces of the code. When it works, the server says so with a special number.

sections.title: Protecting the Data Channel
sections.content:
Before protecting file transfers, client and server agree on a buffer size with PBSZ. Its argument is a decimal integer, the maximum size in bytes of encoded blocks, and it must fit in a 32-bit unsigned integer. There is no default, and the client must send PBSZ before its first PROT. If the size is too large for the server, the reply uses PBSZ=number to offer a smaller one, and both sides use the smaller.

PROT then sets the protection level with a single character. The default is Clear. A mechanism may offer fewer levels, or give more protection than the level asks for.

Protection is applied after the usual representation type, file structure and transfer mode transformations, treating the data as a byte stream. The sender splits the stream into blocks so that each encoded block is no larger than the negotiated size. Each encoded block is sent with its length prepended as a four byte unsigned integer, most significant byte first. At end of file the sender encodes a block of zero bytes and sends it before closing the data connection. The receiver reads a length, reads that many bytes, decodes and verifies the block, and repeats until it sees the zero-byte block.

Checks apply to individual blocks, not the whole file, so inserted or replayed blocks could go undetected. The RFC says the chosen mechanism should guard against this.

A server answers 534 to STOR, STOU, RETR, LIST, NLST or APPE if the protection level is below what its policy requires for that transfer, and 535 if any protection service fails during the transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: Big files are cut into pieces. Each piece goes into its own sealed envelope with its size written on the front, and an empty envelope at the end means, that is all.

sections.title: Protected Commands and Replies
sections.content:
Three commands carry a protected FTP command as base 64 text: MIC (integrity), CONF (confidentiality) and ENC (both, called privacy). The server decodes and verifies the message and then treats it as an ordinary FTP command.

Replies use a new 6yz class: 631 for integrity protected, 632 for confidentiality and integrity protected, and 633 for confidentiality protected. The client decodes and verifies the reply. A protected reply may be sent only after a successful security data exchange.

A protected multiline reply is broken into fragments. Each fragment is protected, then base 64 encoded into its own line, formed as the reply code, a hyphen, then the encoded fragment. Line breaks in the encoded reply need not match the plaintext.

To stop an attacker inserting or deleting commands on the control stream, once a security exchange succeeds with a mechanism that supports integrity, integrity protection must be used until the client sends CCC, which must itself be protected. After CCC succeeds, an unprotected command gets an unprotected reply. The RFC says use of CCC is not recommended and exists for interoperability, and gives IP security as a setting where it could make sense.

Recommendations in the RFC: once a security exchange has taken place, a server should require all commands to be protected and protect all replies. A client should encrypt PASS whenever possible, and a server may refuse an unencrypted PASS if it knows encryption is available.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of speaking out loud, each command is written on a note and locked in a box. The server unlocks it, checks nobody changed it, and answers in a locked box too.

sections.title: Security Mechanisms and Base 64
sections.content:
Every protected message, and every ADAT argument, is base 64 encoded, so it uses only characters safe on the Telnet-based control connection. Input is processed in 24-bit groups, each becoming 4 characters from the 64-character set [A-Z][a-z][0-9]+/, with = as padding. Line breaks must not be included. Because encoded lines can be arbitrarily long, an implementation must read the whole line, which may take several reads, and must not reject a well-formed command only because it is long. Case matters when reading base 64.

The appendices define two mechanisms. The GSSAPI mechanism, named GSSAPI in AUTH, is preferred for new mechanisms because existing FTP implementations then need little change and other protocols can reuse it. The client names the service as ftp@hostname with the fully qualified host name in lower case, and may retry with host@hostname. MIC and 631 map to wrapping without confidentiality, ENC and 632 to wrapping with it, and CONF and 633 are not supported.

The Kerberos version 4 mechanism is named KERBEROS_V4. The client gets a ticket for the principal ftp.hostname@realm (falling back to rcmd), and the server proves itself by returning the authenticator checksum plus one, signed. CONF and 633 are not supported here either. A cleartext buffer grows by 31 bytes with krb_mk_safe and by 26 bytes with krb_mk_priv, which implementors must allow for within the PBSZ limit.
sections.plainLanguage: Base 64 is a way to write any secret scribble using only ordinary letters and digits, so it survives the trip. The appendices say exactly how two known lock types, GSSAPI and Kerberos, plug in.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC says the whole document deals with security considerations for FTP. It names one gap: third-party file transfers cannot be secured with these extensions. A security context cannot be set up between two servers, because there is no control connection between them to carry ADAT tokens. Further work in this area was deferred.

Other limits come from the design itself. No functionality is required, so a mechanism may do only integrity, one-way authentication, or encryption alone, and a peer may demand more protection than the other offers, which prevents perfect interoperability. Block-by-block checks mean replay protection depends on the mechanism chosen. A server that does not want to reveal that a mechanism exists may answer 504 instead of 534.
sections.plainLanguage: The lock works when you talk to one server. It cannot yet protect two servers passing a file between themselves, because they have no way to share a secret first.
